implementation_notes: Rust's Iterator is the pattern with static dispatch: iter()/into_iter() produce a lazy iterator, adapters (map, filter, filter_map, flat_map, scan, take, zip, chain) return new iterator types, and a consumer (collect, fold, sum, count, for_each, find, any) drives them. The std::iter documentation calls such functions 'iterator adapters', stresses that they are lazy - 'nothing really happens until you call next' - and notes that counting, summing or folding can be implemented more efficiently than by repeated next. Collecting into Vec/HashMap (or into Result for fallible chains) is the materialising terminal, and the whole chain typically optimises to the hand-written loop.
code_sketch:
let emails: Vec<&str> = people
    .iter()
    .filter(|p| p.active)
    .map(|p| p.email.as_str())
    .take(10)
    .collect();                 // terminal: nothing ran before it

let total: u32 = orders.iter().map(|o| o.amount).sum();
pitfalls: Iterators are lazy: a chain built only for its side effects never runs (the compiler warns about an unused map) - use a for loop or for_each.
Adapters consume the iterator (into_iter moves the collection), so borrowing elements while the iterator is alive fights the borrow checker; materialise to release the borrow.
Collecting into a Vec allocates even when only a scalar is wanted, and pushing into a growing Vec reallocates repeatedly - pre-size with Vec::with_capacity or use the right consumer.

variants.name: rayon parallel iterators
variants.implementation_notes: rayon's ParallelIterator mirrors the adapter vocabulary - par_iter()/into_par_iter(), map, filter, flat_map, fold, reduce, sum, collect - and runs the stages over a work-stealing pool; the trait documentation shows chained par_iter().filter().reduce() and notes that iterating a range in parallel is as simple as into_par_iter(). The Send/Sync bounds on closures rule out data races at compile time, but reduce still combines arbitrary splits, so the combining function must be associative. It replaces the sequential chain only for large, CPU-bound, independent work.
pitfalls: Order is not preserved by parallel adapters: use indexed operations or collect into an ordered container when the result order matters.
Every closure, item and captured variable must be Send/Sync: Rc, Cell or a &mut capture forces a redesign (Mutex, channels) instead of a one-word switch.
rayon's parallel overhead dominates small inputs; it also needs the rayon dependency and an MSRV-compatible toolchain.
